paras: The threatened lynching of Charles Smith and Alfred Green occurred in August 1920 in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, when citizens of New Holland and Intercourse raised lynching threats against the two Black men, who were charged with robbery. Officials placed the men in the Lancaster county jail on August 9 to prevent the threats from being carried out, and no violence against them was reported.

Smith and Green, described in the Philadelphia Evening Public Ledger as "Welsh mountain negroes," were charged with robbing a number of homes along the main line and holding up farmers on their way to market. According to the Lancaster dispatch, both men "have criminal records," a claim it did not attribute to any source.

On the night of August 8, state police captured the two men after what the dispatch called "a spectacular chase" through New Holland, and reported that both were armed. Residents of New Holland and the nearby village of Intercourse then raised "lynching threats" against them; the headline attributed the threats to farmers. The next day the men were moved to the Lancaster county jail, which the report said was done to keep the threats from being carried out.
The coverage does not show whether a crowd gathered or any attempt was made on the jail, and no report of a hearing or trial was found.

The only report found was a short Lancaster dispatch on the front page of the Philadelphia Evening Public Ledger on August 9, headlined "SAVED FROM LYNCHERS" with the deck "2 Welsh Mountain Negroes Locked Up When Farmers Threaten." The dispatch presented the robbery charges as charges but added the police account of an armed capture and the unsourced statement about the men's criminal records, without naming any of those who made the threats. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.
